paper_title: Therapeutic Garden With Contemplative Features Induces Desirable Changes in Mood and Brain Activity in Depressed Adults
abstract: The therapeutic values of contact with nature have been increasingly recognized. A growing body of evidence suggests that a unique subcategory of “contemplative landscapes” is particularly therapeutic. Previous studies predominantly focused on observational designs in non-clinical populations. It is not known if these effects can be extrapolated to populations suffering from depression, and experimental designs need to be utilized to establish causality. We examined the effects of in-situ passive exposure to three urban spaces on brain activity, namely a Therapeutic Garden with high Contemplative Landscape scores (TG), Residential Green (RG) and Busy Downtown (BD), and self-reported momentary mood in adults aged 21–74 (n = 92), including 24 clinically depressed and 68 healthy participants. Portable, multimodal electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) systems were used to record brain activity, and a Profile of Mood States (POMS) questionnaire was used to record mood before and after exposure. We tested the interactions between the site, time and group for the mood, and between site and group for the neuroelectric oscillations and brain hemodynamics. Self-reported pre- post-mood was significant only at the TG (p = 0.032) in both groups. The lowest Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) was reported at TG and the highest in BD (p = 0.026). Results from fNIRS indicated marginally significant lower oxy-Hb in the frontal region at TG as compared to BD (p = 0.054) across both groups. The marginally significant effect of site and group was also observed (p = 0.062), with the Clinical group showing much lower oxy-Hb at TG than Healthy. The opposite pattern was observed at BD. EEG results showed differences between Healthy and Clinical groups in the Frontal Alpha Asymmetry (FAA) pattern across the sites (p = 0.04), with more frontal alpha right in the Clinical sample and more left lateralization in the Healthy sample at TG. Temporal Beta Asymmetry (TBA) analyses suggested that patients displayed lower bottom-up attention than Healthy participants across all sites (p = 0.039). The results suggest that both healthy and depressed adults benefitted from exposure to TG, with possibly different pathways of mood improvement. Visiting therapeutic nature with contemplative features may provide valuable support for the treatment of depression in clinical populations and a self-care intervention in non-clinical populations.
methodology: The study employed an in-situ passive exposure experimental design. Participants were exposed to three distinct urban spaces, with the order of location visits and site exposure randomized using a Latin square design to avoid bias. Momentary mood changes were assessed using the Profile of Mood States (POMS) questionnaire, administered before and after exposure to each site. Brain neuro-electrical activity and hemodynamics were measured using a multimodal setup consisting of EEG and fNIRS systems. EEG data was recorded using a 16-channel V-amp amplifier with dry active electrodes, filtered (50 Hz notch, 40 Hz low-pass, 0.5 Hz high-pass), referenced to an average, and ocular artifacts removed via Independent Component Analysis (ICA). Power density values for alpha (8-13 Hz) and beta (14-30 Hz) bands were extracted and baseline-corrected. fNIRS data was collected using two portable NIRx® SPORT devices with eight sources and eight detectors each, mounted in a prefrontal-occipital montage. Oxy-Hb signals were analyzed, with motion artifacts corrected using the CBSI method and short-term physiological noises removed via a moving average method. Environmental variables (temperature, humidity, brightness, noise) were recorded at each scene, and air pollution data (24h Pollutant Standards Index) was retrospectively derived. Data analysis primarily utilized Linear Mixed Models (LMM) to examine differences in mood, hemodynamics, and neuro-electrical activity across groups and sites, accounting for individual variations.

clinical_group.diagnosis: 17 patients diagnosed and treated for depressive disorder, 7 reclassified from healthy due to previous depression treatment/moderate-severe depression

sample.fnirs_analysis_sample: 78 participants (55 Healthy, 23 Clinical) due to signal quality issues

manipulated_features.name: Therapeutic Garden (TG)
manipulated_features.description: Part of a larger park (HortPark), designed for restoration from stress and mental fatigue. Intimate green space with wide-canopy trees, groupings of plants to stimulate senses, spaced benches with views toward fascinating landscapes, calming features (watermill, chimes).

manipulated_features.name: Residential Green (RG)
manipulated_features.description: Green roof area of a public housing residential estate (Casa Clementi HDB Estate). Features include paths among lush greenery, garden shelters, pergolas, community farm, biking trail, and children's playground.

manipulated_features.name: Busy Downtown (BD)
manipulated_features.description: Fully urbanized landscape in a central district near Chinatown and a busy Mass Rapid Transit interchange station. Dominated by crowds, high traffic, and infrastructure, with little to no natural elements.

subscales: Negative Emotions (Tension, Anger, Fatigue, Depression, Confusion - TAFDC)
Positive Emotions (Esteem-Related Affect and Vigor - EV)

outcomes.calculation: [(RF-LF)/(RF+LF)] where RF = sum of AFp2, AFF6h, F8 alpha power; LF = sum of AFp1, AFF5h, F7 alpha power
[(RT-LT)/(RT+LT)] where RT = sum of FT8, T8 beta power; LT = sum of FT7, T7 beta power

key_findings.finding: Significant main effect of site, with lowest TMD at TG (M = 91.6, SE = 1.64) and highest at BD (M = 99.1, SE = 1.64).
Clinical sample had significantly higher TMD (M = 97.9, SE = 2.64) compared to Healthy sample (M = 90.8, SE = 1.62).
TMD decreased (mood improved by 2%) after site exposure only at TG in both groups.
TMD increased (mood worsened by ~7%) after site exposure in BD.
Significant main effect of site, with highest negative emotions in BD (M = 14.472, SE = 1.39).
Clinical group (M = 14.09, SE = 2.29) had significantly higher scores than Healthy group (M = 8.41, SE = 1.36).
Significant interaction between site and time, suggesting both groups responded similarly to changes over time across sites.
Negative emotions decreased significantly in both groups, particularly in TG (by 22%).
Marginally significant lower oxy-Hb in the frontal region at TG (M = −0.57, SE = 0.43) compared to BD (M = 0.45, SE = 0.33) across all participants.
Marginally significant interaction between group and site, suggesting different patterns of brain oxidation between Clinical and Healthy groups.
At TG, Healthy sample had higher oxy-Hb (M = 0.34, SE = 0.47) compared to Clinical sample (M = −1.49, SE = 0.72).
At BD, Clinical sample had higher oxy-Hb (M = 0.65, SE = 0.56) than Healthy sample (M = 0.24, SE = 0.37).
Significant interaction between groups and sites, indicating different FAA patterns.
At TG, Clinical sample had right-sided FAA, while Healthy sample had left-sided FAA.
At BD, Clinical sample had left-sided FAA, while Healthy sample had right-sided FAA (with overlapping C.I.).
In RG, both samples showed similar patterns of right-sided FAA activation.
Healthy sample in general had a higher right-sided TBA compared to Clinical sample across all sites.
Healthy sample demonstrated right-sided TBA across all sites, while Clinical sample only had left-sided TBA in BD.

mechanisms: **Therapeutic Garden (TG):** Lower frontal oxy-Hb is associated with restorative effects and reduced rumination, suggesting less cognitive resource allocation. Right-sided FAA in the clinical group at TG aligns with positive approach-related motivation and efficacious depression treatment outcomes. Bottom-up attention (fascination) is triggered, leading to attention restoration and recovery from mental fatigue.

**Busy Downtown (BD):** Increased mood disturbance (TMD, TAFDC) is linked to higher frontal oxy-Hb in patients. Left-sided FAA in the clinical group at BD is consistent with patterns observed in depressed individuals. Lower TBA in patients suggests extra mental fatigue from prolonged exposure to busy urban environments, indicating reduced bottom-up attention.

**General:** Different landscape designs, quantifiable by CLM scores, induce distinct psychophysiological responses. EEG alpha activity patterns can reflect relaxation/creative ideation or boredom/fatigue, while TBA reflects attentional deployment and restoration.
limitations: Unbalanced sample size between clinical (n=24) and healthy (n=68) groups, though mixed effect models were used.
Higher educational attainment in the study sample compared to the general population, limiting generalizability.
Data collection in a naturalistic setting increases the risk of unmeasured confounding factors, despite controlling for environmental variables.
fNIRS results are highly variable due to factors like melatonin concentration in the skin and low signal quality, requiring cautious interpretation.
Only momentary changes in mood and brain activity were examined; longitudinal data is needed to determine the sustained effects.
Short passive exposure duration (1 minute per scene) might have been insufficient to induce expected attention restoration patterns as measured by TBA.
design_implications: Therapeutic gardens with contemplative features can serve as an effective and affordable supplement for depression treatment and a self-care intervention for mental health maintenance in healthy populations.
Providing easily accessible therapeutic gardens in urban areas can be an important strategy for city-scale mental health promotion.
Therapeutic gardens can potentially offset the negative mental health impacts of busy urban environments.

The specific physical attributes and design of green spaces (as assessed by the Contemplative Landscape Model) are crucial for inducing positive psychophysiological responses, indicating that not all green spaces offer the same therapeutic potential.

environmental_features: elements designed for contemplation (e.g., specific views, quiet zones)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural environments can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue, particularly in individuals with attentional deficits or mental fatigue (e.g., depressed adults).
Exposure to natural environments can reduce physiological and psychological stress more effectively than urban environments, leading to positive affective states.

instruments_used.name: Profile of Mood States (POMS)
instruments_used.construct: mood states (tension, depression, anger, vigor, fatigue, confusion)
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire measuring six distinct mood states.

instruments_used.name: functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS)
instruments_used.construct: prefrontal cortex activity (e.g., oxygenated hemoglobin concentration)
instruments_used.description: A non-invasive optical imaging technique used to measure changes in cerebral blood flow and oxygenation, indicative of neural activity.

instruments_used.name: Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
instruments_used.description: A physiological measure reflecting the variation in the time interval between consecutive heartbeats, often used as an indicator of stress and relaxation.

stimulus_images.description: Photographs of the therapeutic garden environment used as the intervention stimulus
Photographs of the urban street environment used as the control condition
